gloss_terse: Azekah, a fortified city in the Shephelah of Judah near Socoh, associated with battles against Canaanites and Philistines
gloss_readable: Azekah was a strategically important fortified city in the low hills (Shephelah) of Judah, near the town of Socoh. It appears in some of Scripture's most dramatic military narratives: the Israelite pursuit of the Amorite coalition under hailstones (Josh 10:10-11), the valley where David faced Goliath (1 Sam 17:1), and as one of the last two Judean strongholds still holding out against Nebuchadnezzar (Jer 34:7). Multilingual renderings consistently transliterate the name directly, reflecting its firm place-name identity across traditions.

senses.1: The fortified city of Azekah in Judah's Shephelah, situated near Socoh overlooking the Valley of Elah. It served as a key military waypoint: Joshua's forces pursued the Amorite kings past it (Josh 10:10-11), David and Saul's armies camped near it against the Philistines (1 Sam 17:1), and Jeremiah names it as one of the final Judean cities resisting Babylon (Jer 34:7). Rehoboam fortified it (2 Chr 11:9) and returnees resettled there (Neh 11:30).

gloss_terse: Achbor, a personal name meaning 'mouse,' borne by an Edomite clan-father and a Judean court official under Josiah
gloss_readable: The name Achbor (meaning 'mouse') belongs to at least two distinct biblical figures. The first is the father of the Edomite king Baal-Hanan (Gen 36:38-39). The second is the father of Elnathan, a courtier in King Josiah's reign who helped retrieve the newly found scroll of the Law (2 Kgs 22:12, 14). The name's zoological meaning is well attested in Northwest Semitic onomastics, paralleling similar animal names in Latin tradition.

senses.1: The proper masculine name Achbor/Akhbor, etymologically linked to the Hebrew word for 'mouse' (עַכְבָּר). It identifies two figures: an Edomite patriarch whose son Baal-Hanan became king (Gen 36:38-39; 1 Chr 1:49), and a Judean courtier under Josiah involved in the consultation of Huldah the prophetess (2 Kgs 22:12, 14). Spanish renders it 'Acbor/Ajbor,' while French and German often retain the Hebrew script, reflecting transliteration variation across traditions.

gloss_terse: Exultant, jubilant; describing cities or persons marked by boisterous, triumphant rejoicing or revelry
gloss_readable: This adjective captures a mood of loud, triumphant exultation, often applied to cities personified as reveling in their prosperity. Isaiah uses it repeatedly to characterize places like Jerusalem and Tyre before their downfall (Isa 22:2; 23:7), and Zephaniah applies it to Nineveh (Zeph 2:15). The word carries an edge of irony in prophetic speech: the jubilation it describes is typically about to be silenced by divine judgment. Spanish 'exultante' and French 'triomphant' both capture the overtone of proud, noisy celebration.

senses.1: Exultant or jubilant, describing a state of boisterous, triumphant rejoicing. Predominantly used in prophetic judgment oracles where cities are personified as reveling before their fall: Jerusalem as the 'jubilant city' (Isa 22:2), ancient Tyre (Isa 23:7), and Nineveh (Zeph 2:15). Also describes persons in Isa 13:3 ('my proudly exulting ones') and the silencing of revelers' noise in Isa 24:8. The prophetic context gives it an ironic or ominous tone: exultation that is about to be cut short.

gloss_terse: A young woman of marriageable age; maiden, with connotations of virginity in many traditions (cf. Isa 7:14)
gloss_readable: This noun designates a young woman who has reached the age of marriage, carrying strong connotations of youth and, in many translation traditions, virginity. Its most famous occurrence is Isaiah 7:14, where the Septuagint rendered it with Greek parthenos ('virgin'), shaping centuries of messianic interpretation. Elsewhere it appears naturally: Rebekah at the well (Gen 24:43), Miriam watching baby Moses (Exod 2:8), and young women in festive processions (Ps 68:25). The plural form appears in Song of Songs for the 'maidens' who love the bridegroom (Song 1:3).

senses.1: A young woman of marriageable age, typically unmarried and presumed chaste. The term occurs in pivotal narrative moments: Rebekah approaching the well (Gen 24:43), young Miriam watching over Moses (Exod 2:8), and most consequentially in Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy (Isa 7:14), where the LXX translation as parthenos shaped Christian theology. Spanish 'doncella' and French 'jeune fille' both emphasize youthful femininity. The plural appears in festive and romantic contexts: maidens in procession (Ps 68:25) and the beloved's admirers in Song of Songs (1:3; 6:8).

gloss_terse: Amos, the 8th-century prophet from Tekoa, a herdsman called to prophesy against Israel's social injustice
gloss_readable: Amos is the name of the shepherd-prophet from Tekoa in Judah who was called by God to deliver oracles of judgment against the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II. His name, possibly meaning 'burden-bearer,' suits his role as the bearer of heavy prophetic pronouncements against social oppression and empty ritual. All seven occurrences fall within the book that bears his name, and every major translation tradition renders it identically as Amos.

senses.1: The proper name of the prophet Amos (עָמוֹס), a herdsman and dresser of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah (Amos 7:14), active around 760-750 BC. He confronted the priest Amaziah at Bethel (Amos 7:10-12) and delivered oracles emphasizing justice and righteousness. The name is consistently transliterated across all traditions: English, Spanish 'Amos,' French 'Amos,' and German 'Amos,' reflecting the prophet's universal recognition in biblical literature.

gloss_terse: Branch, bough; the limb of a tree or vine, used literally and in prophetic imagery of growth and judgment
gloss_readable: This noun refers to a branch or bough of a tree, used both in everyday agricultural instruction and in rich prophetic symbolism. Leviticus 23:40 prescribes taking branches of thick trees for the Feast of Booths. Ezekiel employs the word powerfully in his allegory of the cedar (Ezek 17:23) and the vine (Ezek 17:8), and in the promise that Israel's branches will again bear fruit (Ezek 36:8). Malachi's final chapter warns that the coming day will leave the wicked neither root nor branch (Mal 3:19).

senses.1: A branch or bough of a tree or vine, used both concretely and figuratively. In literal usage, Leviticus 23:40 prescribes gathering leafy branches for Sukkot. Prophetically, Ezekiel uses it in his vine and cedar allegories: the transplanted vine sending out branches (Ezek 17:8), the majestic cedar sheltering nations (Ezek 17:23; 31:3), and the promise of renewed fruitfulness for Israel's mountains (Ezek 36:8). Malachi's image of neither root nor branch remaining (Mal 3:19) represents total destruction. Spanish 'rama' and French 'branche' directly mirror the concrete botanical sense.

gloss_terse: Ezion-geber, an ancient port city at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba near Elath, used as a wilderness station and later a naval base
gloss_readable: Ezion-geber was an important port city located at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, near the town of Elath. It served first as a station during Israel's wilderness wanderings (Num 33:35-36; Deut 2:8) and later as Solomon's shipbuilding and trading port for voyages to Ophir (1 Kgs 9:26). Jehoshaphat's ill-fated fleet was wrecked there (1 Kgs 22:48). Multilingual renderings consistently transliterate the compound name, though with phonetic variation reflecting each language's conventions.

senses.1: The port city of Ezion-geber (עֶצְיוֹן גֶּבֶר) at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, near Elath. It first appears as a wilderness encampment site during the exodus journey (Num 33:35-36; Deut 2:8). Under Solomon, it became a major naval base where ships were built for trade with Ophir (1 Kgs 9:26; 2 Chr 8:17). Jehoshaphat later attempted to revive this maritime enterprise, but the ships were destroyed (1 Kgs 22:48; 2 Chr 20:36). Spanish 'Ezion-Geber/Etsion-Gueber' and French 'Etsyon-Gever' show the phonetic adaptation across traditions.

gloss_terse: Striped, streaked; describing the markings on Jacob's sheep and goats in the breeding narrative
gloss_readable: This adjective describes animals with visible stripes or streaks in their coloring, appearing exclusively in the Jacob-Laban livestock narrative of Genesis 30-31. It refers to the distinctively marked sheep and goats that became Jacob's wages through his divinely guided breeding strategy. Spanish 'rayado/rayadas' and German 'gestreift' precisely capture the visual sense of streaked or striped patterning. The word is always used alongside related terms for speckled and spotted animals, forming a vocabulary cluster for livestock markings.

senses.1: Striped or streaked in color, used exclusively of sheep and goats in the Jacob-Laban breeding account (Gen 30:35-40; 31:8, 10, 12). The adjective describes animals with visible bands or lines in their fleece or hide, distinguishing them from the speckled (נָקֹד) and spotted (טָלוּא) animals also mentioned. Jacob's divinely guided strategy produced these striped animals as his rightful wages. Spanish 'rayado' and German 'gestreift' both convey the linear pattern precisely, while French uses the English loanword 'striped.'

gloss_terse: To be sweet, pleasing, or agreeable; of sleep, meditation, desires, and sacrificial offerings being pleasant to someone
gloss_readable: This stative verb expresses the quality of being sweet, pleasing, or delightful to someone. It spans sensory and spiritual domains: sleep that is sweet (Prov 3:24; Jer 31:26), meditation that is pleasing to God (Ps 104:34), and sacrificial offerings that either please or fail to please the Lord (Jer 6:20; Mal 3:4; Hos 9:4). The negative uses are particularly striking, as prophets declare that Israel's offerings are not sweet to God because of their unfaithfulness. Spanish 'agradable' and French 'doux' reflect the dual register of pleasantness and sweetness.

senses.1: Qal stative verb meaning to be pleasing, sweet, or agreeable to someone. It governs a range of subjects: sleep that is sweet after labor (Prov 3:24; Jer 31:26), the psalmist's meditation pleasing to God (Ps 104:34), a realized desire being sweet to the soul (Prov 13:19), and a person being pleasing to another (Ezek 16:37). Several prophetic uses negate it regarding sacrifices: Israel's offerings 'are not pleasing to me' (Jer 6:20; Hos 9:4), contrasted with the future day when Judah's offering 'will be pleasing' (Mal 3:4). Spanish 'agradable/dulce' and French 'doux' capture both the gustatory and relational dimensions.

gloss_terse: Oreb, a Midianite prince slain by Ephraim at the rock that bears his name during Gideon's campaign
gloss_readable: Oreb is the name of one of two Midianite princes (the other being Zeeb) captured and executed by the Ephraimites during the pursuit following Gideon's dramatic night victory over the Midianite camp. He was killed at a rock that subsequently bore his name, 'the rock of Oreb' (Judg 7:25). The event became a paradigm of God's decisive deliverance: Isaiah recalls it as 'the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb' (Isa 10:26), and the psalmist invokes it as a prayer for similar victory (Ps 83:11).

senses.1: The proper name Oreb (עֹרֵב, homophonous with 'raven'), identifying a Midianite prince captured and killed by the Ephraimites at a landmark rock during Gideon's campaign (Judg 7:25; 8:3). The place of his execution became known as 'the rock of Oreb,' and the victory became a type-scene of divine deliverance referenced by Isaiah (Isa 10:26) and in Psalm 83:11. Spanish and English consistently render it 'Oreb/Orev,' while French occasionally shows 'soir' (an erroneous association with the homonym for 'evening'), and German preserves 'Oreb.'
